nameStory: The 'lady crab' gets its feminine moniker from its elegant, delicate appearance compared to bulkier crab cousins. The scientific name 'ocellatus' means 'spotted with little eyes,' referring to the distinctive eye-like spots that dot this crab's beautiful shell.
description: The Ocellate Lady Crab is a gorgeous swimming crab with a flattened, oval-shaped shell decorated with eye-like spots and intricate patterns. These medium-sized crabs typically measure 2-4 inches across their shell and have a distinctly feminine, graceful appearance. Their shells display beautiful calico patterns in shades of gray, brown, and purple, earning them the alternate name 'calico crab.' Unlike many crabs that scuttle along the bottom, lady crabs are excellent swimmers with paddle-shaped back legs.

idTips.label: Eye-like spots
idTips.description: Look for distinctive circular spots with darker rings that resemble tiny eyes scattered across the shell - these 'ocelli' give the crab its scientific name and are unique among New England crabs

idTips.label: Flattened oval shell
idTips.description: The shell feels smooth to the touch and is noticeably wider than it is long, creating an oval profile that's more streamlined than typical round crab shells

idTips.label: Paddle-shaped hind legs
idTips.description: The last pair of legs are flattened like tiny paddles rather than pointed - you can feel the broad, flat surface that helps them swim through the water

idTips.label: Calico coloration
idTips.description: The shell displays a beautiful mottled pattern of grays, browns, and purples that feels slightly rough like fine sandpaper when dry

idTips.label: Sharp spines on shell edge
idTips.description: Run your finger carefully along the shell's edge to feel 5-6 sharp spines on each side - these feel like tiny thorns and can prick unwary fingers

habitat: Ocellate Lady Crabs prefer sandy and muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters, from the low tide line down to about 150 feet deep. You'll find them in protected bays, harbors, and coastal waters throughout New England, often buried in soft sediment during the day. They're commonly caught in crab traps or occasionally found washed up on sandy beaches after storms.

seasonality.spring: Lady crabs become more active as waters warm, moving into shallower areas to feed and beginning their mating season in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most commonly caught by recreational crabbers and frequently seen in shallow waters. Females may be carrying bright orange egg masses.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters as temperatures cool. This is often when the largest specimens are caught.
seasonality.winter: Lady crabs retreat to deeper waters and become less active, rarely encountered in shallow areas during the coldest months.

funFact: Lady crabs are such strong swimmers that they can actually swim backwards faster than they can scuttle forwards on land - their paddle-like hind legs work like tiny propellers to jet them through the water in reverse!
confusionNotes: Lady crabs are most often confused with blue crabs, but lady crabs have distinctive eye-spots and an oval shell, while blue crabs have a more triangular shell and bright blue claws. Remember: 'Ladies have lovely eye-lashes' - those eye-spots are the giveaway!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'lady crabs,' both males and females look quite similar, unlike some crab species where males and females are dramatically different. The name reflects their delicate appearance rather than any gender-specific characteristics.
compareHints: The Ocellate Lady Crab is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making identification easier once you learn its key features. Compared to other swimming crabs in the region like blue crabs, lady crabs are distinguished by their oval shell shape, distinctive eye-spots, and more subdued coloration. While blue crabs have aggressive, bright blue claws, lady crabs have more uniform, mottled coloring throughout their body and claws.
